### Focal adhesion TIRF imaging

μ-Slides (iBidi) were coated with FN (5 μg/ml) in PBS at 4°C overnight. Next, μ-Slides were gently washed once with cold PBS following incubation with EV or sEV at 4°C overnight. The following day, μ-Slides were incubated with 0.1% BSA in PBS for 30 min at 37°C to block non-specific binding sites and washed with PBS three times, and 250 μl of M199 media supplemented with 20% sEV-free FBS was added to each well. VSMCs were incubated in M199 media supplemented with 0.5% BSA overnight, detached with trypsin and resuspended to 80,000 cells/ml in M199 supplemented with 20% FBS. Cells (250 μl) were added to μ-Slides and were incubated for 30 min at 37°C. VSMC were fixed with 4% PFA for 10 min at 37°C, washed with PBS three times and were permeabilised with PBS supplemented with 0.2% Triton X-100 for 10 min at 37°C. Next, VSMC were washed three times with PBS for 5 min and were incubated with 3% BSA in PBS for 1 hr at room temperature. VSMC were incubated with anti-vinculin antibody (1:400) in blocking buffer at 4°C overnight. Next, VSMC were washed with PBS for 5 min and incubated with secondary antibody (1:500, AlexaFluor488) diluted in blocking buffer for 1 hr at room temperature. Cells were incubated with CellMaskRed (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and DAPI (0.1 mg/ml) for 5 min, washed and analysed by TIRF microscopy.

TIRF microscopic images were collected on a Nikon Ti2 upright microscope with a TIRF illuminator (Nikon) attached using a 100x oil immersion (1.49 NA) objective lens. In each fluorescent channel, the sample was excited with a laser beam at an angle indicated as follows (488 nm at 62.3°, 561 nm at 62.5°, and 640 nm at 65.5°). All emission light was filtered through a quad channel filter set (Chroma 89000) in the upper filter turret and a secondary bandpass emission filter in the lower turret position was used as follows for each channel (488 nm excited: filter BP 525/50 - Chroma; 561 nm excited: filter BP 595/50 - Chroma; 640 nm excited: filter BP 700/75 - Chroma). Light was then passed to a Hamamatsu Orca-Flash 4v3.0 sCMOS camera and exposures for channels were set as follows (488 nm: 100ms, 561 nm: 100ms, 640 nm: 50ms) with 16bit channel images collected.

Acquisition was all controlled through NIS-Elements software (Nikon). Analysis of TIRF images was completed using NIS-Elements General Analysis Module. A general description of the process follows: Cell Area measurements were determined by use of an intensity threshold on the HCS CellMask Deep Red channel at an intensity of 100 AU (grey levels or arbitrary units) above the background to mask the cell. The Cell area, whole cell Vinculin and Far-Red intensity measurements were calculated from this binary region. In addition, an inversion of the cell mask binary was generated to have a means to measure distance to edge of the cell.

Vinculin-derived foci were masked using an intensity-based threshold (Above 10000 AU) and a size minimum for objects was set to 0.5 µm2 to eliminate smaller non-foci objects from the binary mask. The foci mask was then limited to the cell mask regions to allow interpretation of the foci in the cell area. Minimum distance to the outside of the cell for each foci was calculated by measurement of the nearest distance to the inverted non-cell mask. The average distance was then recorded for each image. For each foci intensity measurements were taken for the Vinculin and FarRed channel and the Mean intensity of the foci was recorded.

### 2D VSMC migration time-lapse assay

24-well plates were incubated with FN (5 µg/ml) in PBS overnight at +4°C and treated with sEVs (10 µg/ml) diluted in PBS overnight at +4°C. VSMC (8000 cells per well) were plated on the plate in M199 supplemented with 20% sEV-free FBS and incubated for 16 hr. Cells were washed twice with DMEM supplemented with 2.5% sEV-free FBS and incubated in this media for 2hrs +/-3’-OMS. Media was replaced for a fresh aliquot and cells were imaged using Opera Phenix High Content Screening System (PerkinElmer) every 6 min 20 s for 8 hr in a transmitted light channel. Quantification of cellular velocity and directionality was performed in Harmony 4.9 (Perkin Elmer) and the following filters were applied to the raw data: ‘Number of Timepoints’ ≥ 5, ‘First Timepoint’ <5.

### 3D VSMC invasion time lapse assay

#### Acquisition

Migration assay was completed using IBidi Chemotaxis µ-slides (Ibidi µ-slides #80326). VSMC were deprived overnight in M199 supplemented with 0.5% BSA, counted and mixed with Matrigel supplemented with/without sEV (5 µg total in 100 µl volume) to a final cell concentration of ca. 3x106 cells/ml and stained with Draq5 according to the manufacturer protocol. Slides were left for 30 min at 37°C for gelation and chemoattractant-free medium (65 µl of M199 supplemented with 0.5% BSA) was filled through Filling Port E. Next, the empty reservoir was filled by injecting chemoattractant medium (65 µl of M199 supplemented with 20% FBS sEV-free FBS) through Filling Port C. Three slides were loaded and cells were imaged with the Opera Phenix (Perkin Elmer) high content imaging platform (10x Objective NA 0.3). Images were collected for digital phase contrast and a fluorescence channel for Draq5. Fluorescence was obtained by exciting with a 640 nm laser and emission light was filtered with a 700/75 bandpass filter to a sCMOS camera. Images were recorded every 10 min for 12 hr in several locations for each slide.

#### Migration tracking and analysis of tracking

Analysis of cell motion was completed on Draq5 images using Harmony Software (Perkin Elmer) with measurements of cell area, speed and direction obtained for each cell/track and timepoint. Cells were not selected for tracking if they were in proximity to other cells at a distance of 35 µm. The measurements and object data were exported and further analysis was performed. Data for each track included total length (timepoints), speed (µm/s), Straightness, accumulated distance (µm), lateral displacement (µm), and vertical displacement (µm).

#### Data analysis

This data was then analysed using an in-house script using Python library Pandas (https://github.com/Alex-biochem/eLife-VOR-RA-2023-90375, copy archived at Kapustin, 2025). Tracks were discarded if they were less than 3 time-points in length. Means and Standard Deviations were calculated for track length (timepoints), Speed (µm/s), Track Straightness and accumulated distance. For each track, the Parallel FMI (forward motion index) was calculated by taking a ratio of vertical displacement to accumulated distance. The means and standard deviations for these were calculated and reported for each condition similarly. Track straightness is calculated as the ratio of total displacement over total track length. Accumulated distance is the total length of the track from the first to last time point of the track.

### Clinical samples

#### Patients enrollment

The study was approved by the Local Ethical committee of the Research Institute for Complex Issues of Cardiovascular Diseases (Kemerovo, Russia, protocol number 20200212, dates of approval: 12 February, 2020), and a written informed consent was provided by all study participants after receiving a full explanation of the study. The investigation was carried out in accordance with the Good Clinical Practice and the Declaration of Helsinki. Criteria of inclusion were: (1) performance of carotid endarterectomy due to chronic brain ischaemia or ischaemic stroke; (2) a signed written informed consent to be enrolled. A criterion of exclusion was incomplete investigation regardless of the reason; in this case, we enrolled another subject with similar age, gender, and clinicopathological features who met the inclusion criteria. Cerebrovascular disease (chronic brain ischaemia and ischaemic stroke) as well as comorbid conditions (arterial hypertension, chronic heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, overweight, and obesity) were diagnosed and treated according to the respective guidelines of European Society of Cardiology, Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease, Global Initiative for Asthma, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes, American Diabetes Association, and European Association for the Study of Obesity. eGFR was calculated according to the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation. Extracranial artery stenosis was assessed using the color duplex screening (Vivid 7 Dimension Ultrasound System, General Electric Healthcare). Data on age, gender, smoking status, and pharmacological anamnesis were collected at the time of admission. In total, we enrolled 20 patients. The detailed characteristics of the study samples are presented in Supplementary file 1.

#### Sample collection and preparation

Carotid atherosclerotic plaques (n=14) and adjacent intact arterial segments (n=14) were pairwise excised during the carotid endarterectomy and divided into 3 segments each. The first segment was snap-frozen in the optimal cutting temperature compound (Tissue-Tek, 4583, Sakura) using a liquid nitrogen and was then sectioned on a cryostat (Microm HM525, 387779, Thermo Scientific). To ensure the proper immunofluorescence examination, we prepared 8 sections (7 µm thickness), evenly distributed across the entire carotid artery segment, per slide. The second and third segments were homogenised in TRIzol Reagent (15596018, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for RNA extraction or in T-PER Tissue Protein Extraction Reagent (78510, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplied with Halt protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (78444, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for the total protein extraction according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Quantification and quality control of the isolated RNA was performed employing Qubit 4 fluorometer (Q33238, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Qubit RNA BR assay kit (Q10210, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Qubit RNA IQ assay kit (Q33222, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Qubit RNA IQ standards for calibration (Q33235, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Qubit assay tubes (Q32856, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Quantification of total protein was conducted using BCA Protein Assay Kit (23227, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Multiskan Sky microplate spectrophotometer (51119700DP, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol.

#### Immunofluorescence examination

Upon the sectioning, vascular tissues were dried at room temperature for 30 min, fixed and permeabilised in ice-cold acetone for 10 min, incubated in 1% bovine serum albumin (Cat. No. A2153, Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 hr to block non-specific protein binding, stained with unconjugated mouse anti-human CD81 (M38 clone, NBP1-44861, 1:100, Novus Biologicals) and rabbit anti-human fibronectin (F14 clone, ab45688, 1:250, Abcam) primary antibodies and incubated at 4°С for 16 hr. Sections were further treated with pre-adsorbed donkey anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated (ab150109, 1:500, Abcam) and donkey anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated secondary antibodies (ab150062, 1:500, Abcam) and incubated for 1 hr at room temperature. Between all steps, washing was performed thrice with PBS (pH 7.4, P4417, Sigma-Aldrich). Nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) for 30 min at room temperature (10 µg/ml, D9542, Sigma-Aldrich). Coverslips were mounted with ProLong Gold Antifade (P36934, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Sections were examined by confocal laser scanning microscopy (LSM 700, Carl Zeiss). Colocalisation analysis (n=12 images) was performed using the respective ImageJ (National Institutes of Health) plugins (Colocalisation Threshold and Coloc2). To evaluate the colocalisation, we calculated Pearson’s r above threshold (zero-zero pixels), thresholded Mander’s split colocalisation coefficient (the proportion of signal in each channel that colocalises with the other channel) for both (red and green) channels, percent volume colocalised with each channel, and intensity volume above threshold colocalised with each channel in both neointima and media.

#### Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR)

Reverse transcription was carried out utilising High Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (4368814, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Gene expression was measured by RT-qPCR using the customised primers (500 nmol/L each, Evrogen, Moscow, Russian Federation, Supplementary file 5), cDNA (20 ng) and PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (A25778, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocol for Tm ≥60°C (fast cycling mode). Technical replicates (n=3 per each sample collected from one vascular segment) were performed in all RT-qPCR experiments. The reaction was considered successful if its efficiency was 90–105% and R2 was ≥0.98. Quantification of the CD9, CD63, CD81, COL6A3, EDIL3, CSPG4, TGFBI, FN1, and MYADM mRNA levels in carotid atherosclerotic plaques (n=5) and adjacent intact arterial segments (n=5) was performed by using the 2−ΔΔCt method. Relative transcript levels were expressed as a value relative to the average of three housekeeping genes (ACTB, GAPDH, B2M).

#### Western blotting

Equal amounts of protein lysate (15 μg per sample) of carotid atherosclerotic plaques (n=12), adjacent intact arterial segments (n=12), and plaque-derived sEVs (n=6) were mixed with NuPAGE lithium dodecyl sulfate sample buffer (NP0007, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 4:1 ratio and NuPAGE sample reducing agent (NP0009, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 10:1 ratio, denatured at 99°C for 5 min, and then loaded on a 1.5 mm NuPAGE 4–12% Bis-Tris protein gel (NP0335BOX, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The 1:1 mixture of Novex Sharp pre-stained protein standard (LC5800, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and MagicMark XP Western protein standard (LC5602, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was loaded as a molecular weight marker. Proteins were separated by the sodium dodecyl sulphate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) at 150 V for 2 hr using NuPAGE 2-(N-morpholino)ethanesulfonic acid SDS running buffer (NP0002, Thermo Fisher Scientific), NuPAGE Antioxidant (NP0005, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and XCell SureLock Mini-Cell vertical mini-protein gel electrophoresis system (EI0001, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Protein transfer was performed using polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) transfer stacks (IB24001, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and iBlot 2 Gel Transfer Device (IB21001, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocols using a standard transfer mode for 30–150 kDa proteins (P0 – 20 V for 1 min, 23 V for 4 min, and 25 V for 2 min). PVDF membranes were then incubated in iBind Flex Solution (SLF2020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 1 hr to prevent non-specific binding.

Blots were probed with rabbit primary antibodies to fibronectin or GAPDH (loading control). Horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-rabbit (7074, Cell Signaling Technology) or goat anti-mouse (AP130P, Sigma-Aldrich) secondary antibodies were used at 1:200 and 1:1000 dilution, respectively. Incubation with the antibodies was performed using iBind Flex Solution Kit (SLF2020, Thermo Fisher Scientific), iBind Flex Cards (SLF2010, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and iBind Flex Western Device (SLF2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific) during 3 hr according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Chemiluminescent detection was performed using SuperSignal West Pico PLUS chemiluminescent substrate (34580, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and C-DiGit blot scanner (3600–00, LI-COR Biosciences) in a high-sensitivity mode (12 min scanning). Densitometry was performed using the ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health) using the standard algorithm (consecutive selection and plotting of the lanes with the measurement of the peak area) and subsequent adjustment to the loading control (GAPDH).

#### Shotgun proteomics and proteomics data analysis

Carotid atherosclerotic plaques and adjacent intact arterial segments were excised pairwise during carotid endarterectomy. Tissue segments were homogenised in T-PER Tissue Protein Extraction Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific), supplemented with Halt protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific), for total protein extraction according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Following acetone (Supelco) precipitation to remove T-PER buffer, protein pellets were resuspended in 8 M urea (Sigma-Aldrich) in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (Sigma-Aldrich). Protein concentration was measured using a Qubit 4 fluorometer and QuDye Protein Quantification Kit (Lumiprobe), per manufacturer’s instructions. Each protein sample (10  μg) was incubated with 5 mmol/L dithiothreitol (Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 hr at 37°C, followed by 15 mmol/L iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich) for 30 min in the dark at room temperature. Samples were diluted with 7 volumes of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and digested for 16 hr at 37°C using trypsin gold (Promega) at a 1:50 trypsin:protein ratio (200 ng per sample). Peptides were dried using a Labconco CentriVap Centrifugal Concentrator (Labconco), dissolved in 0.1% formic acid (Sigma-Aldrich), and desalted with C18 spin tips according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After desalting, peptides were dried again and re-dissolved in 0.1% formic acid for LC-MS/MS analysis. Each sample was analysed in technical duplicate. Approximately 500 ng of peptides were subjected to shotgun proteomics using UHPLC-MS/MS with ion mobility on a TimsToF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) coupled to a nanoElute UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics). Separation was performed in two-column mode using an Acclaim PepMap 5  mm Trap Cartridge and Bruker Ten separation column (C18 ReproSil AQ, 100 mm × 0.75 mm, 1.9  µm, 120  Å; Bruker Daltonics) at a flow rate of 500  nL/min and 50°C. Mobile phase A was water/0.1% formic acid; mobile phase B was acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid. The UHPLC gradient was set as: 2–30% phase B over 16  min, 30–38% phase B over 5  min, and 38–95% phase B over 3  min, followed by 6  min washing at 95% phase B. Electrospray ionisation was achieved using a CaptiveSpray ion source with a capillary voltage of 1600  V, nitrogen flow of 3  L/min, and source temperature of 180°C. Mass spectrometry acquisition was performed in data-independent acquisition mode with trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS, in PASEF mode, diaPASEF). The diaPASEF method included five cycles with three or two mobility windows each, totaling 13 mass width windows (50  Da width) spanning an m/z range of 457.81–1046.80 and ion mobility range (1 /K0) of 0.85–1.18 Vs/cm². Collision energy was programmed as a function of ion mobility, increasing linearly from 20  eV at 1 /K0 = 0.85 Vs/cm² to 59  eV at 1 /K0 = 1.3 Vs/cm². Protein identification was performed using DIA-NN software (v1.8) (Demichev et al., 2020) with the human SwissProt protein database (https://www.uniprot.org; accessed 14 December 2021; taxonomy: Human [9606]; uploaded 2 March 2021). A library-free search was carried out with default settings and the generated library comprised 20,338 proteins and 8,454,641 precursors. Search parameters were set to parent and fragment mass error tolerance of 10 ppm, protein and peptide FDR <1%, and allowance for up to two missed cleavage sites. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was set as a fixed modification.

Further analysis was performed in R (version 3.6.1; R Core Team, 2019). Proteins with missing values in more than two samples were excluded, and remaining missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbours via the impute package. Data was log-transformed and quantile-normalised prior to differential expression analysis with the limma package (Ritchie et al., 2015). Sample clustering was performed using sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis in the MixOmics package (Rohart et al., 2017). Data visualisation utilised the ggplot2 (Wickham, 2011) and EnhancedVolcano (Ubuntu, 2018) packages.

### Statistics

Data were analysed using GraphPad Prizm (version 8.4.3). CD63-beads assay, NanoView, adhesion assay, FA quantification were analysed by one-way ANOVA test. Two group CD63-bead assays were analysed by non-paired T-test. 2D migration multiple comparison data and VSMC invasion multiple comparison data were analysed using non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test. Two group invasion data were analysed using a non-parametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Clinical data for two groups was analysed by non-paired T-test and multiple comparison was analysed by Mann-Whitney U-test. All analysis was conducted using PRISM software (GraphPad, San Diego, CA). Values of p<0.05 were considered statistically significant.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90375.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90375.3.sa1)

In this revised submission from Kapustin et al., the authors have made significant changes to the manuscript. Namely, the authors have addressed several of the major issues with the original submission, providing a more concrete link between fibronectin and the secretion of extracellular vesicles. Additionally, the authors have moderated some of the conclusions to better suit the rigor of the experimental results and limitations of their approach. Generally, the findings convey an interesting cell autonomous pathway in which smooth muscle cells sense fibronectin, which canonically is a proinflammatory substrate with activating properties in many tissues. Fibronectin-mediated integrin signaling stimulates secretion of small extracellular vesicles containing collagen VI which is deposited into the surrounding extracellular matrix. Collagen VI itself gleaned from extracellular vesicle secretion seems to further alter smooth muscle cell morphodynamics. For this later finding, much of the mechanism behind collagen VI vesicle loading and secretion has yet to be worked out. The authors provide evidence of extracellular vesicles containing collagen VI trapped in fibronectin in atherosclerotic plaques providing a nice validation of their in vitro findings in a diseased human cohort. Some limitations do still exist in the manuscript in its current form such as the assessment of the vesicle origins, contents and their association with the actin cytoskeleton; however, the rigor and execution are much improved from the preceding version. Overall, the pathobiology underlying vascular smooth muscle remodeling in disease states is a critical area of research that warrants further exploration.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90375.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90375.3.sa2)

The findings in the current manuscript are interesting and valuable contributions to the fields of vascular biology and extracellular vesicle-related mechanisms. They suggest a potential role for smooth muscle cell-derived extracellular vesicles in presenting Type VI collagen to cells to orchestrate their migration, with proposed relevance to aberrant smooth muscle cell movements in the progression of atherosclerotic lesions. A wide range of assays are utilized to test various aspects of this working model, with the resulting data being largely solid and supporting several of the interpretations articulated by the authors. The revised manuscript has adequately addressed key weaknesses.

The authors present data suggesting a working model in which vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs) are stimulated by fibronectin (FN) to generate small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) that harbor Type VI Collagen (collagen VI). These collagen VI-associated sEVs are suggested to accumulate in the extracellular matrix (ECM) and influence cell migration and adhesion dynamics, potentially contributing to disease progression in atherosclerosis. Majors strengths of this manuscript include robust imaging data and the inclusion of human-derived samples in their analysis. The authors also make a reasonable attempt to provide data to support the potential existence of these mechanistic connections, though some minor questions remain regarding data interpretation. The authors largely achieved their aims of finding evidence consistent with their interpretations, and they have presented logical support for their conclusions while acknowledging important limitations and caveats to their current study. This work will likely have a sustained impact on the field of sEV biology and potential intersections with vascular biology, including their methodology e.g., imaging approaches. As biologists continue to explore the role of sEVs in physiological and pathological processes, this work raises an interesting aspect that must be considered more broadly, and that is, what is the role of sEVs that are ECM-associated and not necessarily internalized by recipient cells? Are there discrete mechanisms that govern their role in maintaining and/or disrupting normal physiological processes? This manuscript makes an attempt to address these unresolved yet critical questions.

results.result: Immobilized fibronectin (FN) and fibrillar collagen I, but not soluble FN or non-fibrillar laminin, stimulate secretion of CD63+/CD81+ small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) by vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). 3D matrices also increase sEV secretion without affecting sEV size distribution or marker composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are supported by multiple experimental approaches including CD63-bead capture assays (C1, C2, C4), nanoparticle tracking analysis (C5), and western blotting (C6). The data consistently show that immobilized/fibrillar ECM components, but not soluble forms, promote sEV secretion. The characterization of sEV markers and size distribution provides additional validation.

results.result: CD63+/CD81+ sEV secretion in response to collagen and FN is regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 (SMPD3), which regulates sEV generation in multivesicular bodies, suggesting a late endosomal origin for these sEVs.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is supported by experimental data using the SMPD3 inhibitor 3-OMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). Claims C8 and C9 are inferences based on this data and prior literature (Trajkovic et al., 2008). The mechanistic link between SMPD3 and late endosomal sEV generation is well-established in the literature, making the inference reasonable.

results.result: FN matrices stimulate sEV secretion via the β1 integrin/FAK/Src signaling pathway. Activation of β1 integrin enhances FN-induced sEV secretion, while inhibition of β1 integrin, FAK, or Src blocks it.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 are supported by experimental data using activating (12G10) and inhibiting (4B4) antibodies for β1 integrin, and small molecule inhibitors for FAK (FAM14) and Src (PP2) (Figure 1G-I). Claim C13 is a reasonable inference from these converging lines of evidence. The specificity of effects on FN-coated versus plastic surfaces strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Arp2/3 inhibition (CK666) reduces sEV secretion on both plastic and FN matrices, while formin inhibition (SMIFH2) is only effective on FN matrix, suggesting formins are involved in FN-dependent sEV secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C15 are supported by experimental data using CK666 and SMIFH2 inhibitors (Figure 2A and B). Claim C16 is a reasonable inference from the selective effect of SMIFH2 on FN matrix. The differential effects of the two inhibitors provide insight into distinct mechanisms of sEV secretion.

results.result: Arp2/3-driven branched F-actin tails are involved in CD63+ multivesicular body (MVB) intracellular transport in VSMCs. Approximately 50% of F-actin tails associate with ~13% of endosomes, and this overlap is enhanced by SMPD3 inhibition with 3-OMS.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 are supported by live cell imaging (Figure 2C, Video 2) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 2D) showing colocalization of F-actin, cortactin, and CD63. Quantitative colocalization analysis (C20, C21) provides statistical support. Claim C22 is a reasonable inference from these data combined with the effects of Arp2/3 inhibitors. However, the authors note these are rare events in live imaging, which may limit the strength of the conclusion.

results.result: CD63+ MVBs are present along Myo10-positive filopodia in both plastic and FN conditions, with anterograde MVB transport toward the filopodia tip observed in live VSMCs, indicative of MVB secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C24 are supported by quantitative analysis and immunofluorescence data (Figure 2E). Claim C25 is supported by live cell imaging (Figure 2F, Video 3). The observation of anterograde transport provides direct evidence for MVB secretion via filopodia, though the authors note in C29 that more studies are needed to confirm this hypothesis.

results.result: sEV secretion by VSMCs is regulated via Arp2/3 and formin-dependent actin cytoskeleton remodeling, with branched actin tails potentially contributing to MVB intracellular transport and secretion at the VSMC-ECM interface. CD63+MVBs can be observed in filopodia-like structures.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by TIRF microscopy data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Video 4) and cited literature (Hoshino et al., 2013). Claim C27 is a reasonable inference from multiple experiments. Claims C28 and C29 are more speculative, with the authors explicitly noting that more studies are needed to confirm the filopodia hypothesis. The overall conclusion is supported but with acknowledged limitations.

results.result: sEVs can bind to the ECM secreted by VSMCs and are trapped in native ECM produced over 7 days. This trapping is reduced when VSMCs are treated with SMPD3 siRNA.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by cited literature (Hutcheson et al., 2016; Whitehead et al., 2023). Claims C31 and C33 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3A, 3B). Claim C32 is a reasonable inference from the observation of sEVs on both plastic and FN-coated surfaces. The data consistently support ECM trapping of sEVs.

results.result: EVs are both loosely bound and strongly trapped within the ECM, with different tetraspanin profiles. The conditioned media and 0.5 M NaCl fraction show high abundance of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs, while the GuHCl fraction is enriched with CD63+ and CD63+/CD81+ sEVs with very low CD9+ EVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by sequential extraction and ExoView analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The differential tetraspanin profiles between fractions suggest distinct EV populations with varying degrees of ECM association. The methodology is appropriate for distinguishing loosely bound from strongly trapped EVs.

results.result: FN is endocytosed and delivered to early and late endosomes, colocalizes with CD63+MVBs, and can be co-purified with sEVs. This colocalization and sEV secretion are reduced in confluent VSMCs, indicating that confluence abrogates intracellular FN trafficking and sEV secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-H) and CD63-bead assays. Claim C43 is a reasonable inference from the correlation between FN trafficking and sEV secretion at different cell densities. The data consistently show that FN is recycled through the endosomal system and secreted via sEVs, with cell density as a regulatory factor.

results.result: FN can be co-purified with sEVs from VSMC conditioned media and is detected on the surface of sEVs by flow cytometry, confirming its loading and secretion via sEVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C45 are supported by western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I) and flow cytometry data (Figure 3C). The use of two independent methods to detect FN on sEVs strengthens the conclusion that FN is a bona fide sEV cargo protein.

results.result: sEVs added to cell media are rapidly taken up by VSMCs and delivered to the nuclear periphery, while sEVs added to FN-coated plates are not internalized even 24 hours after cell addition, with no perinuclear localization observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C46 and C47 are supported by super-resolution microscopy data (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, K). The differential behavior of sEVs in media versus ECM-associated sEVs provides important functional insight into how ECM trapping affects sEV fate and function.

results.result: Unbiased proteomics analysis of atherosclerotic plaques versus intact arterial segments revealed 213 plaque-specific and 111 intact arterial-specific proteins, with 46 proteins significantly overexpressed in plaques. sEV cargo proteins fetuin-A and Apolipoprotein B-100 are elevated in plaques, while the negative regulator of sEV secretion Coronin 1C is downregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by proteomic analysis (Figure 4A-C, Supplementary files). Claim C53 is supported by cited literature (Hutcheson et al., 2016; Tagliatela et al., 2020). The proteomic data provide strong evidence for altered sEV-related protein expression in atherosclerotic plaques, consistent with increased sEV secretion during disease progression.

results.result: FN accumulates in both the neointima and tunica media of atherosclerotic plaques and is significantly colocalized with the sEV marker CD81, particularly in cell-free, matrix-rich regions. The majority of CD81 in the neointima originates from VSMCs rather than endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by immunofluorescence data and quantitative colocalization analysis (Figure 4D-F). Claims C57 and C58 are supported by colocalization analysis with CD31 (Figure 4G) and appropriate statistical analysis. The data provide strong evidence for sEV accumulation in atherosclerotic plaques and their association with FN-rich ECM.

results.result: Western blot analysis confirmed FN accumulation in the plaque region. FN expression could not be detected in plaques or intact vessels by RT-PCR but was abundant in the liver, suggesting that the circulation is a key source of FN in atherosclerotic plaques.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by western blot data (Figure 4H, I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E). Claim C60 is supported by RT-PCR data (though not shown). Claim C61 is a reasonable inference from the RT-PCR results. However, the lack of shown RT-PCR data is a limitation. The conclusion that circulating FN is the primary source is consistent with prior literature.

results.result: FN coating promotes VSMC velocity in a 2D migration model, and inhibition of sEV secretion with 3-OMS reduces VSMC speed. However, addition of sEVs to the ECM has no effect on VSMC speed at baseline but rescues cell speed in the presence of 3-OMS, suggesting sEVs are not primarily regulating cell speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by 2D migration assay data (Figure 5A, B) and cited literature (Sung et al., 2015; Sung and Weaver, 2017). Claim C65 is a reasonable inference from the observation that sEVs have no effect at baseline. The data suggest that sEVs may have a more nuanced role in cell migration than simply promoting speed.

results.result: In a 3D invasion assay, addition of sEVs has no effect on cell speed, accumulated distance, or straightness, but VSMCs invading in the presence of embedded sEVs migrate more aligned to the FBS gradient. This effect is specific to sEVs, as larger EVs have no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by 3D invasion assay data (Figure 5D-H). Claim C69 is a reasonable inference from these results. The data provide strong evidence that ECM-associated sEVs influence VSMC invasion directionality rather than speed, which is a novel and important finding.

results.result: ECM-associated sEVs impair VSMC adhesion to FN. FN alone stimulates VSMC spreading and adhesion, but addition of sEVs stalls adhesion after ~15 minutes, suggesting a defect in cellular spreading. This effect is specific to sEVs, as larger EVs have no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C72, C73, and C75 are supported by adhesion assay data (Figure 6A-C). Claims C71 and C74 are reasonable inferences from these data. The use of both static adhesion assays and real-time xCELLigence monitoring provides strong evidence for the inhibitory effect of sEVs on VSMC spreading.

results.result: FN increases the number of centripetal focal adhesions (FAs) in VSMCs, but addition of sEVs significantly reduces FA number and shifts newly formed FAs to the cell periphery. FA size and turnover are not affected by sEVs, but traction force is increased, suggesting that ECM-associated sEVs trigger formation of FAs with enhanced pulling force at the cell periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 and C82 are supported by TIRF microscopy, FA turnover analysis, and pillar displacement data (Figure 6E-K). Claims C80, C81, and C83 are reasonable inferences from these data. The combination of FA localization, size, turnover, and traction force measurements provides comprehensive evidence for the mechanism by which sEVs modulate cell adhesion.

results.result: Proteomic analysis identified 257 proteins in sEVs and 168 in EVs, with 142 common proteins. The top 5 functional enrichment clusters in sEVs are related to cell migration and adhesion. The cell adhesion cluster includes collagen VI, FN, thrombospondin, EDIL3, and TGFBI, which are predominantly involved in cell-matrix interactions. LGALS3BP is exclusively present in sEVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C85, C86, C88, and C89 are supported by proteomic analysis and western blotting (Figure 7A-C, Supplementary files 6-8). Claim C87 is a reasonable inference from GO pathway analysis. The proteomic data provide strong evidence for a unique adhesion-related protein signature in sEVs.

results.result: Collagen VI is the most abundant protein in VSMC-derived sEVs and is present in sEVs extracted from 3D matrix. Collagen VI was previously implicated in interaction with NG2 and suppression of cell spreading on FN.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by proteomic data (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 7). Claim C93 is supported by western blot data (Figure 7D). Claims C91 and C92 are supported by cited literature (Tillet et al., 2002; Nishida et al., 2018). The data establish collagen VI as a key sEV cargo protein with known roles in cell adhesion.

results.result: Dot-blot analysis reveals that Alix is preferentially a luminal protein in sEVs, CD63 is a surface protein, and collagen VI is distributed with 40% on the outside surface and 60% in the sEV lumen.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by dot-blot data with and without permeabilization (Figure 7E). The methodology is appropriate for determining protein localization on/in sEVs. The finding that collagen VI is partially surface-exposed is important for understanding its functional role.

results.result: Addition of anti-collagen VI antibody restores VSMC spreading on FN matrix. sEVs isolated from VSMCs after collagen VI knockdown have no effect on cell speed or direction in a 3D invasion model but reduce cell alignment to the gradient compared to scrambled siRNA control.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by xCELLigence adhesion assay data (Figure 7F) and 3D invasion assay data (Figure 7G-I). The use of both antibody blocking and siRNA knockdown provides strong evidence for the functional role of collagen VI in sEV-mediated effects on cell adhesion and directionality.

results.result: Collagen VI and TGFBI expression are significantly elevated in atherosclerotic plaques, consistent with increased deposition of sEVs during disease progression.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 7J). Claim C101 is a reasonable inference from the correlation between protein expression and sEV deposition. The data provide in vivo validation of the relevance of collagen VI-enriched sEVs in atherosclerosis.

results.result: The study demonstrates that FN enables VSMC migration and invasion by stimulating secretion of collagen VI-loaded sEVs via β1 integrin activation. These sEVs associate with the ECM and induce early formation of mature peripheral FAs with enhanced pulling force, thus controlling FA formation and cell-ECM crosstalk to modulate cell directionality during invasion.
results.evaluation: These claims represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from multiple experiments. They are supported by converging evidence from sEV secretion assays, proteomic analysis, FA formation studies, traction force measurements, and 3D invasion assays. The mechanistic model is well-supported by the data, though some aspects (e.g., the exact signaling pathways downstream of collagen VI) remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: The study contextualizes its findings within the broader literature on cell migration, focal adhesion dynamics, Rho GTPase signaling, collagen VI biology, and atherosclerosis. Prior work has established FN as a marker of unstable plaques, the role of Rho GTPases in cell spreading and adhesion, and the involvement of collagen VI in various cardiovascular pathologies.
results.evaluation: These claims are all supported by cited literature and provide important context for interpreting the current findings. The authors appropriately cite relevant prior work and position their findings within the existing knowledge base. However, these are primarily literature-based claims rather than novel experimental findings from this study.

results.result: The study proposes several speculative mechanisms and hypotheses that require further investigation, including the role of branched actin tails in MVB transport, sEV secretion via filopodia, the primary role of sEVs in regulating cell speed, and whether collagen VI modulates FA formation through signaling or structural mechanisms.
results.evaluation: These claims are explicitly noted by the authors as speculative or requiring further study. While they are reasonable hypotheses based on the observed data, they lack sufficient direct experimental evidence to be considered supported. The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations.

results.result: Extensive secretion of sEVs effectively ceases protrusion activity and VSMCs acquire a rounded morphology when 'hovering' over the FN matrix decorated with sEVs.
results.evaluation: This claim is based on observations that are mentioned but for which data are not shown. Without access to the supporting data, it is difficult to evaluate the strength of this claim. The observation is plausible given the other findings but requires validation.

results.result: Fibronectin (FN) and collagen I, but not soluble FN or laminin, stimulate secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs by VSMCs via β1 integrin/FAK/Src signaling pathways and sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 (SMPD3), indicating a late endosomal origin for these sEVs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors 'have addressed several of the major issues with the original submission, providing a more concrete link between fibronectin and the secretion of extracellular vesicles.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the resulting data being largely solid and supporting several of the interpretations articulated by the authors.' The editor describes the evidence as 'mostly convincing.'

results.result: sEV secretion by VSMCs is regulated via Arp2/3 and formin-dependent actin cytoskeleton remodeling, with branched F-actin tails involved in CD63+MVB intracellular transport and secretion at the VSMC-ECM interface, and MVBs observed in filopodia-like structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'some limitations do still exist in the manuscript in its current form such as the assessment of the vesicle origins, contents and their association with the actin cytoskeleton.' This indicates that while data are presented, the mechanistic connection between actin structures and sEV secretion remains incompletely resolved.

results.result: sEVs bind to and are trapped in the ECM secreted by VSMCs, with different populations (loosely bound vs. strongly trapped) showing distinct tetraspanin profiles. FN is endocytosed, colocalizes with CD63+MVBs, and is loaded onto sEVs. ECM-associated sEVs are not internalized by cells, unlike media-added sEVs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the resulting data being largely solid and supporting several of the interpretations articulated by the authors' and notes 'robust imaging data' as a major strength. The editor describes the evidence as 'mostly convincing.' These findings on sEV-ECM interactions are central to the manuscript's model.

results.result: Proteomic analysis of human atherosclerotic plaques reveals FN accumulation and colocalization with CD81+ sEVs in neointima and tunica media, particularly in cell-free, matrix-rich regions. FN originates from circulation (liver) rather than local vessel expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors provide evidence of extracellular vesicles containing collagen VI trapped in fibronectin in atherosclerotic plaques providing a nice validation of their in vitro findings in a diseased human cohort.' Reviewer 2 highlights 'the inclusion of human-derived samples in their analysis' as a major strength. The editor states the paper 'will be valuable for researchers investigating cell migration during vessel repair and atherogenesis.'

results.result: ECM-associated sEVs have modest influence on VSMC speed but significantly influence VSMC invasion directionality in 3D models, with sEVs promoting alignment to gradients. This effect is specific to sEVs and not observed with larger EVs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the resulting data being largely solid and supporting several of the interpretations articulated by the authors.' Reviewer 1 notes the findings 'convey an interesting cell autonomous pathway' and that 'collagen VI itself gleaned from extracellular vesicle secretion seems to further alter smooth muscle cell morphodynamics.' The directional migration data support the proposed mechanism.

results.result: ECM-associated sEVs impair VSMC adhesion and spreading on FN by inducing early formation of peripheral focal adhesions (FAs) with enhanced traction force, without affecting FA size, turnover, or stability. This effect is specific to sEVs and not observed with larger EVs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'a wide range of assays are utilized to test various aspects of this working model, with the resulting data being largely solid.' Reviewer 1 states 'collagen VI itself gleaned from extracellular vesicle secretion seems to further alter smooth muscle cell morphodynamics.' The FA analysis data are described as robust by the reviewers.

results.result: Proteomic analysis reveals that VSMC-derived sEVs are enriched in cell adhesion proteins, with collagen VI being the most abundant protein. Collagen VI is present both on the sEV surface (40%) and in the lumen (60%), and is found in ECM-associated sEVs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors provide evidence of extracellular vesicles containing collagen VI trapped in fibronectin in atherosclerotic plaques.' Reviewer 2 states 'the resulting data being largely solid and supporting several of the interpretations.' The proteomic characterization is central to the mechanistic model and appears well-supported.

results.result: Collagen VI presented by sEVs is essential for early peripheral FA formation and VSMC invasion directionality. Anti-collagen VI antibody restores VSMC spreading, and collagen VI knockdown reduces cell alignment in 3D invasion. Collagen VI and TGFBI expression are elevated in atherosclerotic plaques.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'the authors provide evidence of extracellular vesicles containing collagen VI trapped in fibronectin in atherosclerotic plaques providing a nice validation of their in vitro findings.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors largely achieved their aims of finding evidence consistent with their interpretations.' The collagen VI functional data with antibody blocking and knockdown experiments support the mechanistic conclusions.

results.result: The overall model: FN enables VSMC migration and invasion by stimulating secretion of collagen VI-loaded sEVs via β1 integrin/FAK/Src and Arp2/3-dependent pathways. These sEVs associate with the ECM and control FA formation and cell-ECM crosstalk, with α5β1 integrin functioning as an ECM sensor.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'the findings convey an interesting cell autonomous pathway in which smooth muscle cells sense fibronectin...Fibronectin-mediated integrin signaling stimulates secretion of small extracellular vesicles containing collagen VI.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors largely achieved their aims of finding evidence consistent with their interpretations, and they have presented logical support for their conclusions.' The editor describes the evidence as 'mostly convincing.'

results.result: Discussion and contextual claims about cell migration mechanisms, Rho signaling, collagen VI biology, and connections to atherosclerosis and other cardiovascular diseases, largely supported by literature citations.
results.evaluation: These claims are primarily literature-based contextual information and discussion points. Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors have presented logical support for their conclusions while acknowledging important limitations and caveats to their current study.' The reviewers do not challenge these contextual claims, which are well-supported by citations.
